derivations.claim: Draw $M$ codewords independently from $P_X^{\otimes n}$. For a received $y^n$, declare message $m$ if it is the unique codeword whose information density exceeds $\ln(M-1)+\tau$; if there is no unique such message, output a fixed default. The first event has probability exactly the miss probability in the Statement. For one competing word $\bar X^n$ independent of $Y^n$, the latter has density $q^{\otimes n}$ under the ensemble. The nonnegative likelihood ratio $L:=\prod_t w(Y_t\mid\bar X_t)/q(Y_t)$ has expectation
$$\mathbb EL=\int P_X^{\otimes n}(d\bar x^n)\int q^{\otimes n}(y^n)\frac{w^{\otimes n}(y^n\mid\bar x^n)}{q^{\otimes n}(y^n)}\,d\nu^{\otimes n}(y^n)=1$$
by [F1, F2] and normalization of each channel row.

If a competitor passes, [F3] makes $L>(M-1)e^\tau$, hence the event is contained in $\{L\ge(M-1)e^\tau\}$. Markov's integral inequality [F4] bounds this probability by $e^{-\tau}/(M-1)$. The finite union bound [F5] over the $M-1$ competitors contributes at most $e^{-\tau}$. Combining this with the miss event in step 1.1 proves the asserted bound on ensemble expected average error.

Averaging over the transmitted message and the random codebook gives expected average error at most the displayed bound from steps 1.1 and 2.1. A nonnegative random variable has some value no greater than its expectation; otherwise its expectation would be strictly larger. Selecting such a codebook proves the deterministic-code assertion.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

On $(0,1)$, [F3] gives $h''(t)=-1/t<0$, so [F4] makes $h$ concave there. For $u,v\in[0,1]$ and $0<\epsilon<1$, replace each endpoint by $u_\epsilon=(1-\epsilon)u+\epsilon/2$ and $v_\epsilon=(1-\epsilon)v+\epsilon/2$. Concavity on $(0,1)$ applies to these interior points; taking $\epsilon\downarrow0$ and using step 1.1 gives the concavity inequality on the closed interval.

For $p,q\in\Delta_m$ and $0\le\theta\le1$, apply the concavity inequality for $h$ to each coordinate $\theta p_i+(1-\theta)q_i$. Summing the $m$ inequalities gives $H(\theta p+(1-\theta)q)\ge\theta H(p)+(1-\theta)H(q)$. Continuity of $H$ follows from continuity of the finite sum of the coordinate functions $h$.

Each summand $-p_i\ln p_i$ is nonnegative because $0\le p_i\le1$, so $H(p)\ge0$. The average of the $m!$ coordinate permutations of $p$ is the uniform vector $u=(1/m,\ldots,1/m)$, and each permutation has entropy $H(p)$. Concavity from step 3.1, iterated over this finite average, gives $H(u)\ge H(p)$. Since $H(u)=\ln m$, the claimed upper bound follows, including $m=1$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $P,Q$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
([[def-probability-measure]]). Absolute continuity $P\ll Q$ has the convention
of [[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]. If
$P\not\ll Q$, define $D(P\|Q)=+\infty$. If $P\ll Q$, assume AC
([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) as in [[def-likelihood-ratio-as-rn-derivative]] and
let $r=dP/dQ$ be a finite-valued nonnegative measurable representative of its
Radon–Nikodym class; such a representative exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].
On $\{r=0\}$ set $\ell=0$, and on $\{r>0\}$ set $\ell=\log r$. This
function is measurable: for $a\ge0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r>\exp(a)\}$, and for
$a<0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r=0\}\cup\{r>\exp(a)\}$, by the inverse and
monotonicity properties of the natural logarithm
([[def-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]). These are
measurable sets by [[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Since
$P(\{r=0\})=\int_{\{r=0\}}r\,dQ=0$ by
[[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]], the value chosen there does not
affect $\int\ell\,dP$. Define
$$D(P\|Q):=\int \ell\,dP,$$
where $\log$ is the natural logarithm ([[def-natural-logarithm]]).

The definition is independent of the representative: two representatives
agree $Q$-almost everywhere, hence $P$-almost everywhere. Put
$$\psi(0):=0,\qquad \psi(t):=t\log t\quad(t>0).$$
The function $\psi$ is continuous at zero: for $s\ge1$,
$$0\le \frac{\log s}{s}=\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{u}\le\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{\sqrt u}\le\frac2{\sqrt s}.$$
Thus $t\log t\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$; here $L=\log$ by
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]] and
[[def-integral-logarithm]]. On $(0,\infty)$, $\psi$ is a product of continuous
functions by [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], so $\psi$ is continuous on
$[0,\infty)$ and $\psi(r)$ is measurable by
[[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Its signed integral is
defined by the positive and negative parts
([[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]],
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]).

For $0<t\le1$, the function $-t\log t$ has derivative $-\log t-1$ and
maximum $1/e$ at $t=1/e$: $e=\exp(1)>1$ by
[[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]] and
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], $1/e=\exp(-1)$ by
[[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], and $\log(1/e)=-1$ by
[[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and the inverse definition. The mean value
theorem gives increase before and decrease after this point
([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-integral-logarithm-derivative-and-normalisation]],
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]], [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]).
At $t=0$ the negative part is zero. Since $Q$ is a probability measure,
$$\int \psi(r)^-\,dQ\le\frac1e.$$
The change-of-measure identity of [[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]],
applied to $\ell^-$ gives $\int\ell^-\,dP=\int\psi(r)^-\,dQ\le1/e$,
so $\int\ell\,dP$ is well-defined; applying it to both positive and negative
parts gives
$$D(P\|Q)=\int\ell\,dP=\int\psi(r)\,dQ=\int r\log r\,dQ,$$
with $0\log0:=0$ and a finite negative part. Therefore the extended integral
is well-defined without an $\infty-\infty$ ambiguity.

This convention is directional: the first argument must be absolutely
continuous with respect to the second for the integral formula to apply.

Assume AC and use the directional convention of
[[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]]. For probability measures $P,Q$ on one
measurable space, $D(P\|Q)\ge0$, and $D(P\|Q)=0$ if and only if $P=Q$.

There is also the following normalized-density identity. Let
$(\mathsf X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a sigma-finite measure space: it is a set
with a sigma-algebra and measure ([[def-measure-space]]), and there is a
countable measurable cover by sets of finite $\mu$-measure

**Least-upper-bound property.** Every nonempty set $S$ of Dedekind cuts that is
bounded above (there is a cut $B$ with $A \le B$ for all $A \in S$) has a least
upper bound $\sup S$, and it is given explicitly by the union
$$C := \bigcup_{A \in S} A.$$
Together with [[thm-reals-dedekind-ordered-field]] this shows $\mathbb{R}$ is a
**complete totally ordered field**: the Dedekind construction is order-complete.
This order-completeness is the Dedekind counterpart of the Cauchy-sequence
completeness of $\mathbb{R}$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].
$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-x^2}\,dx=\sqrt\pi.$$

Let $I$ and $J$ be intervals, possibly open at finite or infinite singular ends, and let $\phi:I\to J$ be a monotone differentiable surjection. Assume $\phi'$ is locally Riemann integrable and the proper change-of-variable hypotheses hold on every compact truncation. If $f$ is locally Riemann integrable on $J$, then
$$\int_J f(x)\,dx\quad\text{and}\quad\int_I f(\phi(t))|\phi'(t)|\,dt$$
converge simultaneously and, when convergent, are equal. At several singular ends this assertion is applied separately to the corresponding ends; orientation is retained for decreasing parametrizations.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $u, v : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at
every point of $[a,b]$ as functions on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]). Suppose
$u'$ and $v'$ are integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then $uv'$
and $u'v$ are integrable and

$$\int_a^b u\,v' \;=\; u(b)v(b) - u(a)v(a) \;-\; \int_a^b u'\,v .$$

**The integrability of $u'$ and $v'$ is a hypothesis, not a formality.** Without
it the two integrals in the display need not exist at all, and the identity is
then not false but ill-formed; that is
the false statement that deletes it on the companion
page. The hypothesis is automatic when $u$ and $v$ are continuously
differentiable, since a continuous function on $[a,b]$ is integrable
([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]).

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ and every real $a>0$,
$$\frac{x^m}{\exp(ax)}\longrightarrow0\qquad(x\to+\infty).$$

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$

claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis

**Everything is proved through

no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.

followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

common probability space, and let $g_i:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be Borel
measurable for each $i<n$.

$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-x^2}\,dx=\sqrt\pi.$$

For $p_j>0$, substituting $Y_j=X_j+Z_j$ in the log-density ratio gives $\imath_j=\frac12\ln(1+p_j/\lambda_j)-Z_j^2/(2\lambda_j)+(X_j+Z_j)^2/(2(p_j+\lambda_j))$. If $p_j=0$, the information density is identically zero, which agrees with the formula; for finitely many branches, $(\sum_j\imath_j)^2\le d\sum_j\imath_j^2$, so the summed density has mean $I=\frac12\sum_j\ln(1+p_j/\lambda_j)$ and finite variance.

$K=(K(y\mid x))_{x\in\mathcal X,y\in\mathcal Y}$ such that

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Fix an integer $d\ge1$ and a real symmetric positive-definite matrix $K\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$. The **$d$-dimensional additive Gaussian channel with power budget $P\ge0$** has input and output spaces $\mathbb R^d$ and single-use law
$$Y=X+Z,\qquad Z\sim N_d(0,K),\qquad Z\perp X.$$
At each use a fresh independent copy of $Z$ is added, so the channel is memoryless. The input cost is $c(x)=\|x\|_2^2$. A length-$n$ deterministic code with $M$ equiprobable messages meets the **average block power constraint** $P$ when
$$\frac1{nM}\sum_{m=1}^M\sum_{t=1}^n\|x_t(m)\|_2^2\le P.$$
Rates are measured in nats per vector use. The noise law is [[def-multivariate-normal-law]]; positive definiteness of $K$ gives the Lebesgue density stated in [[thm-nondegenerate-multivariate-normal-law-has-density]]. The scalar case $d=1$ is the real AWGN channel. Rates use the natural logarithm [[def-natural-logarithm]].

Assume AC [[def-axiom-of-choice]] and use the channel in [[def-parallel-gaussian-channel-with-power-constraint]] with dimension $d$ and budget $P$. A length-$n$ code with $M\ge1$ equiprobable messages is a tuple of Borel encoders
$$f_t:[M]\times(\mathbb R^d)^{t-1}\to\mathbb R^d,\qquad 1\le t\le n,$$
and a Borel decoder $g:(\mathbb R^d)^n\to[M]$. At time $t$ the input is $X_t=f_t(M,Y^{t-1})$ and the output is $Y_t=X_t+Z_t$, with the fresh independent Gaussian noise of the channel definition. The code meets the expected average-power constraint when
$$\frac1n\mathbb E\left[\sum_{t=1}^n\|X_t\|_2^2\right]\le P.$$
Its average error is $\Pr[g(Y^n)\ne M]$ and its rate is $n^{-1}\ln M$ nats per vector use. If every $f_t$ is independent of $Y^{t-1}$, the code does not use feedback. Define $C_{\rm fb}(P)$ as the supremum of rates $R$ for which feasible feedback codes for all sufficiently large $n$ have average error tending to zero and $\liminf n^{-1}\ln M_n\ge R$. Define $C_{\rm nf}(P)$ by restricting to codes that do not use feedback. Both capacities use natural-log nats per vector use [[def-natural-logarithm]].

Assume AC. Let $K\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ be symmetric positive definite and let $Z\sim N_d(0,K)$ be the additive noise in [[def-parallel-gaussian-channel-with-power-constraint]]. Then there are an orthogonal matrix $U$ and positive numbers $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_d$ such that $K=U^T\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_d)U$ and the coordinates of $UZ$ are independent with laws $N(0,\lambda_j)$. For every input $X$, $\|UX\|_2=\|X\|_2$ and $U(X+Z)=UX+UZ$, so this change of coordinates preserves the power constraint and the channel law.

Assume AC. Let $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_d)$ have independent coordinates $Z_j\sim N(0,\lambda_j)$ with $\lambda_j>0$, and let $X$ be an independent finite-support random vector in $\mathbb R^d$ with $\mathbb E\|X\|_2^2\le P$. Define $I(X;X+Z)$ as the relative entropy, in nats, of the joint law with respect to the product of its marginals. Then
$$I(X;X+Z)\le C_d(P):=\max_{p_j\ge0,\,\sum_jp_j\le P}\frac12\sum_{j=1}^d\ln\left(1+\frac{p_j}{\lambda_j}\right).$$
The maximum is attained by the allocation in [[lem-water-filling-optimal-allocation]].

Let $L\ge1$, let $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_L>0$, and let $P\ge0$. For allocations $p_j\ge0$ with $\sum_jp_j\le P$, set
$$F(p_1,\ldots,p_L):=\frac12\sum_{j=1}^L\ln\left(1+\frac{p_j}{\lambda_j}\right).$$
If $P=0$, the maximum is $0$ at $p_j=0$. If $P>0$, there is a unique $T>\min_j\lambda_j$ solving
$$\sum_{j=1}^L(T-\lambda_j)^+=P,$$
and the maximum is attained at $p_j^*=(T-\lambda_j)^+$. Its value is
$$C_L(P)=\frac12\sum_{j=1}^L\ln^+\left(\frac{T}{\lambda_j}\right),$$
where $u^+=\max(u,0)$ and $\ln^+(u)=\max(\ln u,0)$. The value function $C_L$ is nondecreasing and concave on $[0,\infty)$.

Let $a\in\mathbb R$, let $f:[a,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ be finite and concave, and let $U$ be an integrable real random variable with $U\ge a$ almost surely and $f(U)$ integrable. Then $\mathbb E f(U)\le f(\mathbb E U)$.

Let $M$ be uniform on $[N]$ with $N\ge2$, and let an observation $Y$ have conditional densities $p_m$ with respect to a common measure. Put $q=N^{-1}\sum_m p_m$ and define the posterior $\pi_m(y)=p_m(y)/(Nq(y))$ wherever $q(y)>0$. For every measurable decoder $g(Y)$ with error probability $e=\Pr[g(Y)\ne M]$,
$$H(M\mid Y)\le H(M\mid g(Y))\le h_2(e)+e\ln(N-1)\le\ln2+e\ln N,$$
where $h_2(e)=-e\ln e-(1-e)\ln(1-e)$ with $0\ln0=0$.

Assume AC. For the channel in [[def-parallel-gaussian-channel-with-power-constraint]], let the noise eigenvalues be $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_d>0$. Let $P>0$ and choose $p_j\ge0$ with $\sum_jp_j<P$. Then every rate
$$0\le R< I(p):=\frac12\sum_{j=1}^d\ln\left(1+\frac{p_j}{\lambda_j}\right)$$
is achievable by deterministic no-feedback codes meeting average block power $P$ and with average error tending to zero.

Assume AC. Let $d\ge1$, $m\in\mathbb R^d$, and let $\Sigma$ be a real symmetric positive-definite $d\times d$ matrix. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then its law has Lebesgue density
$$f_{m,\Sigma}(x)=(2\pi)^{-d/2}\det(\Sigma)^{-1/2} \exp\!\left(-\tfrac12(x-m)^T\Sigma^{-1}(x-m)\right), \qquad x\in\mathbb R^d.$$

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Fix an integer $d\ge1$ and a real symmetric positive-definite matrix $K\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$. The **$d$-dimensional additive Gaussian channel with power budget $P\ge0$** has input and output spaces $\mathbb R^d$ and single-use law
$$Y=X+Z,\qquad Z\sim N_d(0,K),\qquad Z\perp X.$$
At each use a fresh independent copy of $Z$ is added, so the channel is memoryless. The input cost is $c(x)=\|x\|_2^2$. A length-$n$ deterministic code with $M$ equiprobable messages meets the **average block power constraint** $P$ when
$$\frac1{nM}\sum_{m=1}^M\sum_{t=1}^n\|x_t(m)\|_2^2\le P.$$
Rates are measured in nats per vector use. The noise law is [[def-multivariate-normal-law]]; positive definiteness of $K$ gives the Lebesgue density stated in [[thm-nondegenerate-multivariate-normal-law-has-density]]. The scalar case $d=1$ is the real AWGN channel. Rates use the natural logarithm [[def-natural-logarithm]].

Assume AC. Let $K\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ be symmetric positive definite and let $Z\sim N_d(0,K)$ be the additive noise in [[def-parallel-gaussian-channel-with-power-constraint]]. Then there are an orthogonal matrix $U$ and positive numbers $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_d$ such that $K=U^T\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_d)U$ and the coordinates of $UZ$ are independent with laws $N(0,\lambda_j)$. For every input $X$, $\|UX\|_2=\|X\|_2$ and $U(X+Z)=UX+UZ$, so this change of coordinates preserves the power constraint and the channel law.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n\ge1$, let $Z\sim N_n(0,I_n)$ have independent standard-normal coordinates, and let $U\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ satisfy $U^TU=I_n$. Then $UZ$ also has independent $N(0,1)$ coordinates. Here $I_n$ is the identity matrix and $U$ is orthogonal.

Assume AC and use the finite-dimensional channel of dimension $d$ and covariance $K$ from [[def-parallel-gaussian-channel-with-power-constraint]]. Let $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_d>0$ be the eigenvalues of $K$ and put $\lambda_{\min}:=\min_j\lambda_j$. Both the ordinary no-feedback capacity $C_{\rm nf}(P)$ and the causal-feedback capacity $C_{\rm fb}(P)$ defined in [[def-parallel-awgn-feedback-code]] equal
$$C_K(P)=\max_{p_j\ge0,\,\sum_jp_j\le P}\frac12\sum_{j=1}^d\ln\left(1+\frac{p_j}{\lambda_j}\right)=\frac12\sum_{j=1}^d\ln^+\!\left(\frac{T}{\lambda_j}\right),$$
where $T$ is the unique water level solving $\sum_j(T-\lambda_j)^+=P$ when $P>0$; for $P=0$, $C_K(0)=0$ and all $p_j=0$. Thus feedback does not increase capacity.

derivations.claim: Direct multiplication gives $U^TU=I_2$ and $U^T\operatorname{diag}(1,4)U=\frac12\begin{pmatrix}5&3\\3&5\end{pmatrix}=K$, hence $UKU^T=\operatorname{diag}(1,4)$, so $K$ is positive definite with eigenvalues $1,4$. By [F1] and [F2], $UZ$ has independent coordinates with variances $1,4$. For every input, $\|UX\|_2^2=X^TU^TUX=\|X\|_2^2$ and $U(X+Z)=UX+UZ$.

Since $P=2<4-1=3$, the water level is $T=1+P=3$: the first branch receives $p_1=T-1=2$ and the second receives $p_2=0$. Substitution in [F3] gives capacity $\frac12\ln(1+2/1)+\frac12\ln(1+0/4)=\frac12\ln3$. The orthogonal code correspondence from step 1.1 transfers this value to the original correlated channel.

Let $L\ge1$, let $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_L>0$, and let $P\ge0$. For allocations $p_j\ge0$ with $\sum_jp_j\le P$, set
$$F(p_1,\ldots,p_L):=\frac12\sum_{j=1}^L\ln\left(1+\frac{p_j}{\lambda_j}\right).$$
If $P=0$, the maximum is $0$ at $p_j=0$. If $P>0$, there is a unique $T>\min_j\lambda_j$ solving
$$\sum_{j=1}^L(T-\lambda_j)^+=P,$$
and the maximum is attained at $p_j^*=(T-\lambda_j)^+$. Its value is
$$C_L(P)=\frac12\sum_{j=1}^L\ln^+\left(\frac{T}{\lambda_j}\right),$$
where $u^+=\max(u,0)$ and $\ln^+(u)=\max(\ln u,0)$. The value function $C_L$ is nondecreasing and concave on $[0,\infty)$.

Assume AC and use the finite-dimensional channel of dimension $d$ and covariance $K$ from [[def-parallel-gaussian-channel-with-power-constraint]]. Let $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_d>0$ be the eigenvalues of $K$ and put $\lambda_{\min}:=\min_j\lambda_j$. Both the ordinary no-feedback capacity $C_{\rm nf}(P)$ and the causal-feedback capacity $C_{\rm fb}(P)$ defined in [[def-parallel-awgn-feedback-code]] equal

derivations.claim: If $0<P\le3$, choosing $T=1+P\le4$ makes $p_1=T-1=P$ and $p_2=(T-4)^+=0$, whose sum is $P$. If $P\ge3$, choosing $T=(P+5)/2\ge4$ gives $p_1=(P+3)/2$, $p_2=(P-3)/2$, and their sum is $P$. At $P=0$ both allocations are zero. In each regime [F1] therefore confirms the displayed water level and nonnegative powers.

Substituting the first allocation into the rate formula [F2] gives $\frac12\ln(1+P)$; substituting the second gives $\frac12\ln(T)+\frac12\ln(T/4)=\ln(T/2)=\ln((P+5)/4)$. At the common endpoint $P=3$, both are $\ln2$.

Let $W(y\mid x)$ be a finite DMC with nonempty finite input alphabet $\mathcal X$ ([[def-discrete-memoryless-channel]]). A **letter cost** is a supplied function $c:\mathcal X\to[0,\infty)$ with finite real values. Define
$$c_{\min}:=\min_{x\in\mathcal X}c(x),\qquad c_{\max}:=\max_{x\in\mathcal X}c(x),\qquad \bar c(P_X):=\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}P_X(x)c(x)$$
for each input probability vector $P_X$ ([[def-finite-probability-vector]]). A real number $\Gamma$ is a **feasible cost budget** when $\Gamma\ge c_{\min}$. Costs and budgets are per channel use; all logarithms and rates in this pair use natural units [[def-natural-logarithm]].

For finite $X,Y,Z$ with a joint pmf,

$$H(X,Y|Z)=H(X|Z)+H(Y|X,Z),$$

and

$$I(X;Y,Z)=I(X;Z)+I(X;Y|Z).$$

In particular, $I(X;Y)=H(X)-H(X|Y)=H(Y)-H(Y|X)$. All terms are finite.

For a finite nonempty alphabet of size $m$, let
$$H(p):=-\sum_{i=1}^m p_i\ln p_i,\qquad 0\ln0:=0,$$
on the probability simplex $\Delta_m=\{p\in[0,1]^m:\sum_i p_i=1\}$. Then $H$ is continuous and concave on $\Delta_m$, with $0\le H(p)\le\ln m$.

Fix a finite DMC and cost model from [[def-finite-dmc-cost-model]], with feasible budget $\Gamma$. A length-$n$, $M$-message code from [[def-fixed-length-channel-code]] is **average-cost feasible** if
$$\frac1{nM}\sum_{m=1}^M\sum_{t=1}^n c(x_t(m))\le\Gamma.$$
A rate $R\ge0$ is **average-error achievable under budget $\Gamma$** if there is a sequence of such codes, for all sufficiently large $n$, whose average errors from [[def-fixed-length-channel-code-errors]] tend to zero and satisfy $\liminf_{n\to\infty}n^{-1}\ln M_n\ge R$. The **operational cost-constrained capacity** $C(\Gamma)$ is the supremum of these rates.

For an input probability vector $P_X$, define its expected cost $\bar c(P_X)$ as in [[def-finite-dmc-cost-model]]. The **cost-constrained information capacity** is
$$C_I(\Gamma):=\sup_{P_X:\,\bar c(P_X)\le\Gamma} I(P_X;W),$$
where $I(P_X;W)$ and the unconstrained DMC information capacity use natural-log nats as in [[def-discrete-memoryless-channel-information-capacity]] and [[def-natural-logarithm]]. All rates use natural-log nats ([[def-natural-logarithm]]). This definition uses a supremum; attainment is proved separately.

Let $W$ be a finite DMC with finite nonnegative input cost $c$, and let $\Gamma\ge c_{\min}$. Under the uniform-message average block-cost and average-error conventions of [[def-cost-constrained-dmc-code-and-capacity]], the operational capacity is
$$C(\Gamma)=C_I(\Gamma)=\max_{P_X:\,\mathbb E c(X)\le\Gamma} I(P_X;W),$$
with all rates measured in nats per use.

For every finite DMC and finite nonnegative letter cost with feasible budget $\Gamma$, the feedback operational capacity $C_{\rm fb}(\Gamma)$ defined in [[def-finite-dmc-feedback-code]] equals the ordinary average-error capacity $C(\Gamma)$ in [[def-cost-constrained-dmc-code-and-capacity]]. Thus $C_{\rm fb}(\Gamma)=C_I(\Gamma)$.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

For a finite nonempty set identified with $[k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}$, a **probability vector** is $p=(p_i)_{i=1}^k$ with $p_i\ge0$ and $\sum_i p_i=1$; it is the outcome-weight vector of a finite probability space ([[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]]). Its Shannon entropy in natural units is
$$H(p):=-\sum_{i=1}^k p_i\ln p_i,$$
with $0\ln0:=0$. For probability vectors $p,q$ on the same set $[k]$, the relative entropy is
$$D(p\|q):=\sum_{i:p_i>0}p_i\ln(p_i/q_i),$$
with value $+\infty$ if $p_i>0=q_i$ for some $i$. A matrix $A\in[0,1]^{N\times m}$ is **row-stochastic** when each row sums to one. For a probability row vector $p$ on $[m]$ and a row vector $X\in[0,1]^m$, the dot product $pX^{\mathsf T}=\sum_{i=1}^m p_iX_i$ is the acceptance probability under distribution $p$.

These definitions use finite sets only; entropy is between $0$ and $\ln k$, as proved where needed below.

derivations.claim: An input law is feasible exactly when $0\le p\le\min\{\Gamma,1\}$, and [F2] makes its mutual information $h_2(p)$. If $0\le p\le q\le1/2$ and $p<1/2$, put $\theta=(1-p-q)/(1-2p)\in[1/2,1]$. Then $q=\theta p+(1-\theta)(1-p)$; concavity and symmetry in [F3] imply $h_2(q)\ge\theta h_2(p)+(1-\theta)h_2(1-p)=h_2(p)$. Thus $h_2$ is nondecreasing on $[0,1/2]$.

For any $p\in[0,1]$, concavity and symmetry give $h_2(1/2)\ge\frac12h_2(p)+\frac12h_2(1-p)=h_2(p)$. Therefore the maximum over the feasible interval occurs at $p=\min\{\Gamma,1/2\}$ and equals the displayed formula. Substitution yields $C(0)=0$, $C(1/2)=\ln2$, and $C(1)=\ln2$.
The feedback theorem in [F4] makes the feedback capacity equal to the same ordinary constrained capacity. This identifies the values for all three requested budgets.
